questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) Neither the students / (B) nor their teacher / (C) were present / (D) at the meeting.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: With 'neither…nor', the verb agrees with the subject CLOSEST to the verb. The subject closest to 'were' is 'their teacher' (singular). Therefore, the verb must be singular: 'was' not 'were'. Correction: 'was present'. Trap: Part A is correct ('neither' is the correlative conjunction starter); Part B is correct; Part D is correct (prepositional phrase). The error is in the verb agreement in Part C.

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) He is / (B) one of the best students / (C) that has ever / (D) studied in this school.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: 'One of the + plural noun + who/that' → the verb agrees with the plural noun, not with 'one'. The antecedent of 'that' is 'students' (plural), so the verb must be plural: 'have ever' not 'has ever'. Correction: 'that have ever'. Common trap: people think the antecedent is 'one' (singular) and use 'has', but the relative pronoun 'that' refers back to 'students' (the noun immediately preceding it in such constructions).

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) The jury / (B) have given / (C) its verdict / (D) unanimously.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Rule: When a collective noun (jury, team, committee, class) acts as a SINGLE unit (giving one verdict unanimously), it takes a singular verb AND a singular pronoun. 'Unanimously' signals they act as one body. Error: 'have' (plural) should be 'has' (singular). 'Its verdict' (Part C) is already correctly singular. Correction: 'The jury has given its verdict unanimously.' Trap: Part C 'its' is correct (singular pronoun matching singular collective noun acting as one unit); the error is only in Part B.

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) She told me / (B) that she will / (C) return the money / (D) the following day.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Rule: In reported speech, when the reporting verb is past ('told'), the verb in the reported clause must also shift back (backshift). 'will' (present future) must change to 'would' (past future) in indirect speech. Correction: 'that she would'. Note: Part D 'the following day' is already correctly changed from 'tomorrow' in indirect speech. Error is only in Part B. Trap: 'the following day' (D) is correct; the error is 'will' not changed to 'would'.

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) He has been / (B) working in this office / (C) since three / (D) years.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: 'Since' is used with a POINT IN TIME (a specific moment: since 2020, since Monday, since morning). 'For' is used with a PERIOD OF TIME (a duration: for three years, for two days, for a long time). 'Three years' is a period/duration, so 'for' is required, not 'since'. Correction: 'for three years'. Trap: Part A (present perfect continuous) is correct for ongoing actions; Part B is correct; error is only in Part C ('since' vs 'for').

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) Each of the students / (B) in the two groups / (C) were asked / (D) to submit their assignment.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither' are distributive pronouns/adjectives and always take a SINGULAR verb. 'Each of the students' → singular subject → singular verb 'was' not 'were'. Correction: 'was asked'. Trap: 'in the two groups' (B) is a prepositional phrase and does not affect subject-verb agreement; 'their' (D) can be singular in informal/modern usage referring back to 'each' as gender-neutral; the error is only in Part C.

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) It is essential / (B) that every student / (C) submits the form / (D) before the deadline.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: After expressions of urgency/necessity like 'it is essential/important/necessary/mandatory that…', the verb must be in the SUBJUNCTIVE mood (base form, no -s ending for third person). 'submits' (indicative) → 'submit' (subjunctive). Correction: 'that every student submit'. This is a classic SSC trap where the -s on a singular subject seems right but the subjunctive rule overrides it. Pattern: 'It is essential/important/necessary that S + base verb (no -s).'

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) The number of accidents / (B) on highways / (C) have increased / (D) this year.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: 'The number of + plural noun' takes a SINGULAR verb (because the subject is 'the number', not 'accidents'). 'have' (plural) should be 'has' (singular). Correction: 'has increased'. Compare: 'A number of accidents have occurred' (here 'a number' = many, so plural verb). SSC tests this distinction frequently. 'THE number' = singular; 'A number' = plural. Trap: 'have' (plural) seems to agree with 'accidents' (plural) but the head noun is 'number', not 'accidents'.

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) She is / (B) much superior / (C) than / (D) her classmates in mathematics.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: 'Superior', 'inferior', 'prior', 'senior', 'junior', 'anterior', 'posterior' are Latin comparative adjectives that already contain a comparative meaning. They do NOT use 'than' — they use 'to'. Correction: 'to' not 'than'. Also: these words should not be preceded by 'more' (e.g., 'more superior' is wrong). Correct sentence: 'She is much superior to her classmates in mathematics.' Trap: 'much' (B) can modify comparative adjectives and is correct here; error is only the preposition in Part C.

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error:
(A) Had I known / (B) that you were coming, / (C) I would have / (D) make better arrangements.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Structure: 'Had I known' = third conditional (inverted 'if I had known'). Main clause must be: 'I would have + past participle'. 'make' is base form; it must be the past participle 'made'. Correction: 'made better arrangements'. This is the 'would have + past participle' rule for the third conditional. Trap: 'I would have make' is the error — 'have' must be followed by past participle, not base verb; Part A uses inverted conditional correctly ('Had I known' = 'If I had known'); Part C 'would have' is correctly formed.
